title: The Lighthouse · 1
paragraphs: So what does it mean, what can it all possibly mean? Lily Briscoe asked herself. She had been left on her own, and she was wondering whether she ought to go to the kitchen and get another cup of coffee, or stay where she was. What does it mean?—that was a stock phrase, picked up out of some book, and it only loosely fit what she was thinking. On this first morning with the Ramsays she could not pull her feelings together; all she could do was let a phrase ring out to cover the emptiness in her mind until these mists had cleared. Because really, what did she feel, returning after so many years to find Mrs. Ramsay dead? Nothing, nothing—nothing she could put into words at all.

She had got in late the night before, when everything was dark and mysterious. Now here she was, awake, sitting at her old place at the breakfast table, but by herself. It was very early as well, not even eight o’clock. There was this trip—Mr. Ramsay, Cam and James were going to the Lighthouse. They ought to have left by now; there was the tide to catch, or something of the kind. And Cam wasn’t ready, and James wasn’t ready, and Nancy had forgotten to order the sandwiches, and Mr. Ramsay had lost his temper and slammed out of the room.
“What’s the use of going now?” he’d raged.

Nancy had disappeared. And there he was, pacing back and forth along the terrace in a fury. You seemed to hear doors banging and people calling everywhere in the house. Then Nancy burst in and, glancing around the room in a strange, half-dazed, half-desperate way, asked, “What does one send to the Lighthouse?” She said it as if she were making herself do something she had no hope of ever managing.

What does one send to the Lighthouse, indeed! On any other day Lily could have given her a sensible answer: tea, tobacco, newspapers. But this morning everything felt so extraordinarily strange that a question like Nancy’s—What does one send to the Lighthouse?—flung doors open in your mind, doors that banged and swung back and forth, so that you kept asking, gaping and stupefied, What does one send? What does one do? Why is one sitting here at all?

Alone at the long table among the clean cups (Nancy had gone out again), she felt shut off from everyone else, fit only to keep on watching, asking and wondering. The house, the place, the morning all felt like strangers. She had no ties here, she felt, no connection with any of it; anything at all might happen. And whatever did happen—a footstep outside, a voice calling out (“It’s not in the cupboard, it’s on the landing!” somebody shouted)—came as a question, as if the thread that normally held things together had been snipped and they were drifting about, up here, down there, away, any old how. How pointless it all was, how chaotic, how unreal, she thought, gazing at her empty coffee cup. Mrs. Ramsay dead; Andrew killed; Prue dead as well—she could say it over as often as she liked and it woke no feeling in her. And here we all are, gathered in a house like this, on a morning like this, she said, looking out of the window. It was a lovely, still day.

All at once Mr. Ramsay, passing by, lifted his head and looked her straight in the face with that wild, distracted gaze of his that was also so piercing—as though he were seeing you, for a single second, for the first time and for ever. To get away from him, she pretended to sip from her empty coffee cup—to dodge his demand on her, to push that commanding need aside for one moment more. He shook his head at her and walked on (“Alone,” she heard him say; “Perished,” she heard him say), and, like everything else on this strange morning, the words turned into symbols and wrote themselves across the gray-green walls. If she could only fit them together, she felt, and write them out as a sentence, she would have reached the truth of things. Old Mr. Carmichael came padding quietly in, got his coffee, and carried his cup away to sit in the sun. The strange unreality of it all was frightening, but it was thrilling too. Going to the Lighthouse. But what does one send to the Lighthouse? Perished. Alone. The gray-green light on the opposite wall. The empty places. These were some of the pieces—but how could they be brought together? she asked herself. As though any interruption would shatter the delicate shape she was putting together on the table, she turned her back on the window in case Mr. Ramsay saw her. Somehow she had to get away, to find somewhere to be alone. Then suddenly she remembered. The last time she had sat here, ten years ago, there had been a small pattern of sprigs or leaves on the tablecloth, and she had looked at it in a moment of revelation. She had had a problem about the foreground of a painting. Move the tree to the middle, she had said. That picture she had never finished. All these years it had been knocking around in her head. Now she would paint it. Where had she put her paints? Yes, her paints. She had left them in the hall last night. She would begin right away. She got up quickly, before Mr. Ramsay could turn round.

She brought herself a chair. With her neat, precise, old-maidish movements she set up her easel at the edge of the lawn—not too near Mr. Carmichael, but near enough to be under his protection. Yes, this must have been the very spot where she had stood ten years ago. There was the wall, there the hedge, there the tree. It was a question of how those masses related to one another. She had carried that question in her head all these years. And now it seemed that the answer had come to her: she knew what she wanted to do.

But with Mr. Ramsay bearing down on her, she could do nothing at all. Each time he drew near—he was pacing up and down the terrace—ruin drew near, chaos drew near. Painting was impossible. She bent down; she turned away; she picked up this rag; she squeezed that tube. But all it did was keep him off for a moment. He made it impossible for her to get anything done. For if she gave him the slightest opening—if he caught her free for a moment, or glancing his way for a moment—he would be upon her, saying, as he had last night, “You find us much changed.” Last night he had stood up, come to a halt in front of her, and said just that. The six children, whom they used to nickname after the Kings and Queens of England—the Red, the Fair, the Wicked, the Ruthless—had all sat there, mute and staring, yet she had felt how furious they were underneath. Kind old Mrs. Beckwith had said something sensible. But it was a house full of passions that had nothing to do with one another—she had felt that the whole evening. And on top of all this chaos Mr. Ramsay had stood up, pressed her hand, and said, “You will find us much changed,” and not one of them had stirred or spoken; they had sat there as if they had no choice but to let him say it. Only James (certainly the Sullen one) glowered at the lamp, and Cam wound her handkerchief round and round her finger. Then he reminded them that tomorrow they were going to the Lighthouse. They were to be ready in the hall at half past seven sharp. Then, with his hand on the door, he paused and swung round on them. Didn’t they want to go? he demanded. If they had dared to say no (he had some reason for wanting it), he would have hurled himself tragically backward into the bitter waters of despair. He had such a talent for gesture. He looked like a king in exile. James said yes, doggedly. Cam faltered more miserably. Yes, oh yes, they would both be ready, they said. And it came to her that this was what tragedy was—not funeral palls, dust and the shroud, but children forced into things, their spirits subdued. James was sixteen, and Cam seventeen, perhaps. She had looked around for someone who was not there—for Mrs. Ramsay, presumably. But there was only kind Mrs. Beckwith, leafing through her sketches under the lamp. Then, tired as she was, her mind still rising and sinking with the sea, the taste and smell that a place has after a long absence taking hold of her, the candles flickering before her eyes, she had lost hold of herself and gone under. It was a marvelous starlit night; they heard the waves as they climbed the stairs; the moon took them by surprise, huge and pale, as they passed the landing window. She had fallen asleep at once.

She fixed her clean canvas firmly on the easel as a barrier—a fragile one, but solid enough, she hoped, to keep Mr. Ramsay and his demands at bay. Whenever his back was turned she did her best to look at her picture—that line there, that mass there. But it was hopeless. He might be fifty feet away, he might not say a word to you, might not so much as see you, yet he seeped into everything, he won out, he forced himself on you. He altered everything. The color was lost to her; the lines were lost to her; even with his back to her all she could think was, He’ll be on me in a moment, wanting—something she felt she was unable to give. She put down one brush and picked up another. When were those children going to come? When would they all be gone? she fretted. That man, she thought, her anger mounting, never gave anything; that man only took. Whereas she would be made to give. Mrs. Ramsay had given. Giving and giving and giving, she had died—and left all this behind. Honestly, she was angry with Mrs. Ramsay. Her brush trembling a little between her fingers, she looked at the hedge, the step, the wall. It was all Mrs. Ramsay’s doing. She was dead. And here was Lily, forty-four years old, wasting her time, unable to do anything, standing there pretending to paint—playing at the one thing that was not to be played at—and it was all Mrs. Ramsay’s fault. She was dead. The step she used to sit on was empty. She was dead.

But what was the good of repeating it again and again? Why keep straining after a feeling she simply didn’t have? There was something like blasphemy in doing that. It was all dry: all shriveled: all used up. They should never have invited her; she should never have come. At forty-four you can’t afford to waste your time, she thought. She hated playing at painting. A brush was the one reliable thing in a world of conflict, ruin and chaos—you had no business playing with it, even knowingly; the idea disgusted her. But he forced her to. You won’t lay a finger on that canvas, he seemed to say as he bore down on her, until you’ve given me what I want from you. And here he was, right beside her again, greedy and distraught. Well, thought Lily despairingly, letting her right hand sink to her side, then it would be easier just to get it over with. Surely she could copy from memory the glow, the rapture, the self-surrender she had seen on the faces of so many women (on Mrs. Ramsay’s, for one) when, on an occasion like this, they would blaze up—she could recall the look on Mrs. Ramsay’s face—into a transport of sympathy, of delight in their reward. Why they felt it she could not tell, but plainly it gave them the most perfect bliss that human nature was capable of. Here he was, come to a stop beside her. She would give him what she could.
